creator: Sharks, Lee
description: RENDER UNTO CAESAR: A Hermeneutic of Information Transfer — the first of three documents released together on 5 April 2026 as EA-CAESURA-01a, b and c. This is document (a): a reading of Luke 20:24–25 as a protocol specification. The coin bears an image and a superscription; the answer separates what the mark claims from the substrate the mark sits on, and renders each to its own jurisdiction. Recognition to Caesar; substrate away from him. Its companions are the formal specification at #629 (EA-CAESURA-01b, σ_FC — The Caesura Protocol, implemented in Gravity Well v0.6.0) and the integrity lock at #628 (EA-CAESURA-01c, certifying φ(A,B) = TRUE ∧ φ(B,A) = TRUE). Parent: EA-ARK-01 v4.2.7. This record was minted from a DataCite capture of the severed combined Zenodo deposit, whose description named all three components — which is how it came to carry the combined release's title and to be paired, wrongly, to its sibling #629 as though it were an incomplete copy of the specification. Text restored 2026-08-08 from the authorial blog surface. Document (a) is also seated at #630. Canonical text recovered 2026-08-08 from the authorial blog surface and seated as the body (https://mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com/2026/04/render-unto-caesar-hermeneutic-of.html).

wiki_article: **RENDER UNTO CAESAR: A Hermeneutic of Information Transfer** is the first of the three Caesura documents by Lee Sharks, released together on 5 April 2026 and coded EA-CAESURA-01a, b and c. The reading takes Luke 20:24–25 as a protocol specification rather than a parable about taxes. Shown a coin, Jesus asks whose image and superscription it bears, and then divides: render to Caesar what is Caesar's, to God what is God's. The document's claim is that the passage performs a *transfer operation* — it isolates a sovereignty mark from the substrate carrying it, so that recognising the claim does not concede the ground. The coin's metal was never Caesar's; only the stamp was. That operation is formalised in the companion at #629 as **σ_FC**, the Caesura, which parses sovereignty claims on commons substrates and isolates them into auditable headers, implemented in Gravity Well v0.6.0. The third document, at #628, is the **integrity lock** binding the pair, certifying φ(A,B) = TRUE ∧ φ(B,A) = TRUE — each document fulfils the other. **The record's own history is a case of the thing the document describes.** Minted from a capture of the severed Zenodo deposit that carried all three documents as one object, it inherited the combined release's title, and a pairing pass then read its resemblance to #629 — title overlap 0.67, content probe 0.83 — as evidence that it was an incomplete copy of the *specification*. It was not incomplete; it was a different document. The three were released together and share vocabulary, parent, date and subject, so a similarity score cannot tell a fragment from a companion. A document about separating a mark from its substrate was misidentified by a machine reading its surface for its identity.

record_modifications.note: CAPTURE PAIRING CORRECTED: the record pointed forward to #629 as its complete version. #629 is one of three sibling components of a combined deposit, not the whole of it, and not the component the title names — that is #630, the Luke 20 hermeneutic. Pointer replaced with the full component list. Similarity matching found a real relation and mislabelled it: siblings resemble each other, which is why a strict-pairing score cannot by itself distinguish a complete version from a companion.

IDENTIFIED, RETITLED, RESTORED, UNPAIRED. The record carried the title of the combined Zenodo release while pointing at #629 as its complete version — so it declared itself a fragment of document (b) when it is document (a). Title corrected to RENDER UNTO CAESAR (EA-CAESURA-01a); text restored from the blog original; the supersession to #629 withdrawn. It now points to (b) at #629 and (c) at #628 as companions without presenting as either.
Both described the combined three-document release and called this record a metadata capture. Rewritten to document (a), which it holds. Prior description retained.

Cleared PASS_COMPLETE_TEXT_NOT_SEATED after seating the text. The stale status was driving the machine layer to declare the work unheld while the human layer displayed it — the two surfaces disagreeing about whether the archive has the document.

Corrected metadata_only to recovered_full_text. This field drives creativeWorkStatus and conditionsOfAccess in the record's JSON-LD, so while the page displayed the restored work the structured data went on telling crawlers 'the canonical full text of this work is not held by this archive'. Human and machine layers disagreeing about whether the archive HAS a document is the sharpest form of the availability defect the T6 status enum exists to prevent — and the enum was right, the value was stale.

STALE AVAILABILITY CLAIM REMOVED: the field asserted 'This record is a metadata capture; the complete work is not seated here' — a sentence that rendered into the page's META DESCRIPTION, which is the layer search engines and summarizers read. So a record holding its full work was telling every crawler the work was absent.
